title: Pay Off Your Mortgage Early or Invest? (The 30 Year Math)
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Should you pay off your mortgage early or invest the extra money in the stock market? Which strategy actually makes you wealthier over 30 years?

In this video, we break down the real math behind paying off your mortgage early vs investing in the S&P 500 — and reveal why your mortgage interest rate could completely change the answer.

Meet Ryan and Steve.
Both are 35 years old. Both buy identical $500,000 homes with $400,000 mortgages. And both have an extra $500 every month.
But they make two very different financial decisions.

Ryan chooses to pay off his mortgage early, putting an additional $500 toward his mortgage principal every month.
Steve chooses to invest, putting that same $500 into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund.

We follow both of them for 30 years, comparing their mortgage balances, interest savings, investment growth, and overall wealth.
And here's where things get interesting.
We run the numbers twice.

SCENARIO 1: A 3% MORTGAGE
With a 3% mortgage rate and an assumed 6% annual investment return, Steve finishes approximately $163,000 wealthier than Ryan.
SCENARIO 2: A 7% MORTGAGE
Change the mortgage rate to 7%, keep the same investment return, and Ryan finishes approximately $69,000 ahead.

Same homes. Same extra $500. Same investment assumptions. 
Completely different results.

So, is it better to pay off your house early or invest your money?
The answer depends on more than just stock market returns.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN IN THIS VIDEO
1. How making extra mortgage payments reduces your principal and saves thousands in interest.
2. Why your mortgage interest rate matters when deciding whether to invest or pay off debt.
3. How compound interest can grow your wealth through long-term S&P 500 index fund investing.
4. How a 3% mortgage compares with a 7% mortgage over 30 years.
5. Why paying off your mortgage early isn't always the best mathematical decision.
6. How mortgage amortization affects the amount of interest you pay.
7. Why investment liquidity, financial security, and peace of mind matter just as much as the numbers.
8. Why building an emergency fund, paying off high-interest credit card debt, and taking advantage of your employer's 401(k) match should generally come before aggressively paying down a low-interest mortgage.

Whether you're a first-time homebuyer, a homeowner considering extra principal payments, or someone trying to build long-term wealth through index fund investing, this video will help you understand the trade-offs between mortgage repayment and investing.

title: Why Smart People Make STUPID Money Decisions
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Why do smart people make bad money decisions? Even people who understand budgeting, saving, and investing can fall into financial traps that cost them thousands of dollars. The surprising reason has less to do with intelligence and more to do with how our brains think about money.

In this video, Logical Money explores the psychology of money and four powerful behavioral finance biases that influence how we spend, save, and invest.

Ever spent twenty minutes comparing prices online to save $10, only to blow $200 on a night out? Or convinced yourself that buying something expensive was perfectly reasonable because you "deserved it"? - Well, you're not alone.

Decades of research in behavioral economics show that our brains don't always make logical financial decisions. Even intelligent, financially knowledgeable people can make costly mistakes without realizing what's influencing their choices.

In this video, you'll discover:
1. Mental Accounting: Why a $1,000 bonus feels different from $1,000 in your paycheck, and how this affects your spending and savings.
2. Opportunity Cost Neglect: Why your brain focuses on what you're buying while ignoring what you're giving up, including opportunities to pay off credit card debt or invest for the future.
3. Overconfidence Bias: How excessive confidence can lead to risky investment decisions, unnecessary stock trading, and financial losses.
4. Present Bias: Why spending money today feels more rewarding than saving for retirement, and how research-backed strategies can help you build better financial habits.

We'll explore fascinating research from renowned behavioral economists, including Nobel Prize winner Richard Thaler, and examine studies on investor behavior, financial decision-making, and retirement savings.

Whether you're trying to improve your money management skills, avoid financial mistakes, pay off debt, or make smarter investment decisions, understanding the psychology behind your choices is an important first step.

Because being smart with money isn't about making perfect decisions every single time. It's about making fewer bad ones.

title: America's $40 Trillion Debt Explained in Simple English
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
America's national debt has surpassed $40 TRILLION. But who does the United States actually owe all that money to? China? Banks? American taxpayers? And what would happen if the U.S. government couldn't pay it back? - The answers might surprise you.

As of October 22, 2026, the U.S. national debt stood at approximately $40.4 trillion, according to the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Yet investors around the world continue lending money to the American government. So how does that work? And how much debt is too much?

In this video, Logical Money breaks down America's national debt, the federal budget deficit, Treasury bonds, interest payments, and the risks of government borrowing — all explained in simple English, without complicated economics jargon.

YOU'LL LEARN: 
1. Why the U.S. government keeps borrowing trillions of dollars every year.
2. Who actually owns America's national debt — and why China owns far less than many people think.
3. Why banks, pension funds, foreign investors, and ordinary Americans continue buying U.S. Treasury bonds.
4. How Treasury bills, notes, and bonds allow the government to borrow money and repay investors.
5. How the U.S. refinances its debt by issuing new bonds to repay maturing ones.
6. Why rising interest rates make America's debt increasingly expensive.
7. How the government's interest payments compare with its national defense spending.
8. Why economists compare government debt with GDP instead of looking only at the total amount owed.
9. What could happen if the United States defaults on its debt.
10. Whether raising taxes, reducing government spending, growing the economy, or creating more money could solve America's debt problem.

Here's something most people don't realize: the United States doesn't have to repay its entire national debt at once. The government is constantly paying off old debt while issuing new Treasury securities.
But that doesn't mean borrowing can grow indefinitely without consequences.

According to the Congressional Budget Office, federal debt held by the public is projected to grow from approximately 101% of U.S. GDP in 2026 to around 120% by 2036. And the Government Accountability Office has warned that America's fiscal path is unsustainable without meaningful changes.

So the real question isn't simply whether America can pay off $40 trillion. It's whether the U.S. economy can continue supporting a growing debt burden without higher interest costs, inflation risks, or difficult choices about taxes and government spending.

Whether you're interested in personal finance, investing, Treasury bonds, the Federal Reserve, the U.S. economy, or how government debt affects ordinary Americans, this video will help you understand the logic behind America's national debt.

title: How the Economy Works — Explained Through One Simple Story
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Ever wondered how the economy actually works? Why can you get a pay raise but still feel poorer? Why does the Federal Reserve raise interest rates? And how can one person's spending decisions affect jobs, businesses, inflation, and even the entire US economy?

In this video, we explain how the economy works through one simple story, making complicated economic concepts easy to understand.

Meet Ryan, a manufacturing employee in Ohio who just received a 5% raise. He should be better off financially, right? Except rising prices, higher mortgage rates, and an unexpected economic slowdown are about to change everything.

Through Ryan's story, we'll discover how inflation affects purchasing power, why businesses raise prices, how consumer spending drives economic activity, and how a slowdown can spread from one small coffee shop to thousands of businesses across America.

Along the way, you'll understand how GDP, unemployment, recessions, interest rates, the Federal Reserve, monetary policy, and government spending all connect.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN IN THIS VIDEO
1. How the Economy Works – Understand how consumers, businesses, workers, banks, and the government influence one another.
2. Inflation Explained – Why prices rise, how inflation reduces purchasing power, and the difference between demand-pull inflation and cost-push inflation.
3. Consumer Price Index (CPI) – How the US measures inflation and why your personal cost of living may rise faster than the official inflation rate.
4. Consumer Spending & the Multiplier Effect – Why one person's spending becomes another person's income, and how reduced spending can create a chain reaction.
4. GDP Explained – What Gross Domestic Product measures and why economic growth matters.
5. Unemployment & Recessions – How slowing business activity can lead to layoffs, rising unemployment, and potentially a recession.
6. Interest Rates & Mortgages – Why borrowing becomes more expensive and how higher interest rates affect housing, consumer spending, and business investment.
7. The Federal Reserve & Monetary Policy – How America's central bank uses interest rates to influence inflation, employment, and economic growth.
8. Government Spending & Fiscal Policy – How government spending and taxation can influence businesses, jobs, and economic activity.

THE BIG IDEA
The economy isn't just numbers on a chart or headlines about inflation, GDP, and interest rates - It's millions of people making everyday financial decisions.

When you spend money, someone else earns it. When businesses earn less, they may cut jobs. When unemployment rises, consumer spending can fall further. And when the Federal Reserve or government changes economic policy, those decisions can affect everything from your mortgage payment to your next paycheck.

Once you understand how these pieces connect, economic news starts making a lot more sense.

REFERENCES & FURTHER READING

2. Federal Reserve – Monetary policy, interest rates, inflation, and employment
3. US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) – Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and US economic growth
4. Freddie Mac – Primary Mortgage Market Survey, historical US mortgage rates
5. National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) – US business cycles and recession dating

description:
How does the stock market actually work? What happens when you buy a stock, why do stock prices rise and fall, and how can ordinary Americans build wealth through investing?

In this video, we explain the stock market from the ground up, using simple stories, real-world examples, and financial history to make investing easier to understand.

We begin in the Netherlands in the early 1600s, where merchants faced enormous risks financing trading voyages. That story takes us to the Dutch East India Company and the origins of modern stock ownership.

Then we follow a small pizza business as it raises money from investors, issues shares, goes public through an IPO, and begins trading on the stock market.

Along the way, you'll discover what actually happens when you buy shares of companies like Apple, Microsoft, or Coca-Cola, why stock prices change, and how investors can participate in the long-term growth of businesses.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
1. What stocks and shares actually represent — and what it means to own part of a company.
2. How the stock market works, from the earliest trading companies to today's US stock exchanges.
3. How companies raise money through an Initial Public Offering (IPO).
4. The difference between the primary market and secondary market — and where your money actually goes when you buy a stock.
5. Why stock prices go up and down, and how investor expectations influence market prices.
6. What caused the dot-com bubble and why even great companies can become terrible investments at the wrong price.
7. Why a booming stock market doesn't necessarily mean the US economy is doing well.
8. How investors make money through capital appreciation, dividends, and compounding.
9. How diversification, S&P 500 index funds, and long-term investing can help investors manage risk and build wealth over time.

THE BIG IDEA
When you buy a stock, you're not just buying a number that moves up and down on a screen. You're buying a small piece of a real business — with employees, customers, products, profits, and risks.

Understanding that simple idea changes the way you think about the stock market.

Whether you're completely new to investing, learning about stocks for the first time, or trying to understand how Wall Street and the US financial markets actually work, this video will help you build a stronger foundation.

title: Index Funds vs Mutual Funds vs ETFs vs Hedge Funds — Explained Simply
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Index Funds vs Mutual Funds vs ETFs vs Hedge Funds — what's the difference, and which investment fund is right for you? 

In this video, we explain all four investment options in simple terms, compare their fees and strategies, and show why choosing the right fund can make a huge difference to your long-term wealth.

You might assume that professional fund managers, backed by teams of analysts and expensive research tools, have a better chance of beating the stock market. But the evidence tells a different story. According to S&P Dow Jones Indices' SPIVA research, the overwhelming majority of actively managed large-cap US equity funds have underperformed the S&P 500 over long investment periods.

So, does that mean index funds are always better? 
Are ETFs different from mutual funds? 
And why do wealthy investors use hedge funds?
In this video, we break down the differences without complicated financial jargon.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
1. Mutual Funds Explained — How professional fund managers invest your money, what active management means, and why expense ratios matter.
2. Index Funds Explained — How funds tracking the S&P 500 and other market indexes work, and why passive investing has become so popular.
3. ETFs Explained — What Exchange-Traded Funds are, how they trade on the stock exchange, and how they compare with traditional mutual funds.
4. Hedge Funds Explained — How hedge funds operate, why they use more flexible investment strategies, and what makes them different from ordinary investment funds.
5. Index Funds vs ETFs — Why an index fund can actually be either a mutual fund or an ETF.
6. Investment Fees and Compound Growth — How a seemingly small difference in annual fees can cost you thousands of dollars over time.
7. Long-Term Investing — Why diversification, low costs, and consistency may matter more than trying to predict the next winning stock.

THE $178,000 DIFFERENCE
Imagine investing $100,000 for 30 years in two funds holding exactly the same investments. Both earn 7% annually before expenses.

Fund A charges 1% annually and grows to approximately $574,000.
Fund B charges just 0.05% annually and grows to approximately $752,000.

That's a difference of nearly $178,000, simply because the lower-cost fund leaves more money invested and compounding over time - It's one of the most important lessons in long-term investing: small fees can have enormous consequences.

WHO IS THIS VIDEO FOR?
Whether you're a beginner learning how to invest, a US investor comparing S&P 500 index funds and ETFs, or someone trying to build a diversified long-term investment portfolio, this video will help you understand the choices available.

You don't need to become a Wall Street expert to make informed investment decisions. You need to understand what you're buying, what you're paying, and how your investment strategy fits your financial goals.

What if the money advice you learned as a kid is actually keeping you from building wealth?

Saving money, working hard, getting a stable job, and earning a higher salary all sound like smart financial advice. But what if following these childhood money lessons isn't enough to achieve financial freedom?

Most of us grew up learning how to earn money, save money, and avoid unnecessary spending. But we weren't always taught how to increase our earning potential, manage our income, invest wisely, and turn that income into long-term wealth.

In this video, Logical Money breaks down 7 childhood money lessons that can quietly keep you financially stuck — and explains the missing financial principles that can help you get ahead.

Here's what you'll learn:
1. Why saving money alone won't make you wealthy.
2. Why hard work doesn't always lead to higher income.
3. Why wanting more money isn't necessarily greedy.
4. Why being good at your job isn't always enough.
5. Why earning more doesn't automatically make you richer.
6. Why a stable job shouldn't be your entire financial plan.
7. Why a high salary doesn't necessarily mean you're wealthy.

THE BIGGEST MONEY LESSON
Being financially responsible and building wealth are two different things. Saving money, working hard, and getting a good job are important foundations. But long-term wealth building also requires learning how to increase your income, manage your spending, invest for the future, and accumulate assets over time.

The financial advice you learned growing up wasn't necessarily wrong.
Maybe you just never got the second half.

Whether you're trying to stop living paycheck to paycheck, improve your money habits, start investing, or work toward financial independence, understanding these personal finance principles can help you make smarter financial decisions.

ABOUT LOGICAL MONEY

No get-rich-quick schemes. No financial hype. No unnecessary jargon.
Just the logic behind money.

title: If YOU Are Saving Money, You NEED To Stop!
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
If you’re saving money, you NEED to stop… and ask yourself one question: what exactly are you saving it for?

Saving money is one of the first financial lessons most of us learn.
Earn $100.
Spend $80.
Save $20.
Keep doing that for decades and eventually… you should be rich.
Right? - Not necessarily.

Because saving money and building wealth are not the same thing.
Cash is incredibly useful. It pays your bills, protects you during emergencies, and gives you financial flexibility. But if money is being saved for decades simply to sit as cash, there’s a problem: Inflation gradually reduces its purchasing power.

In this video, Logical Money breaks down:
1. How money actually works.
2. Why money and wealth are different. 
3. How banks create money through lending.
4. How inflation affects your savings.
5. How to think about saving vs investing, emergency funds, cash, assets, and long-term wealth building.

We’ll go from the giant stone money of Yap and ancient systems of debt and credit to modern bank deposits and the Federal Reserve's 2% longer-run inflation goal.
And it all leads to one important distinction:
Money is the tool. Wealth is the valuable things that money ultimately allows you to own.

Think about your money as having three different jobs:
NOW — Money for rent, groceries, utility bills, school fees, everyday spending, and other expenses you need to cover now.
SAFETY — Your emergency fund and money you expect to need relatively soon. 
WEALTH — Money you don't expect to need for years. This is where the objective can change from simply storing dollars to potentially using those dollars to acquire assets.

Before saving another dollar, understand its job.
Is it for next month's rent?
An emergency fund?
A purchase next year?
Or wealth you want to build over the next 20 or 30 years?
Those are very different financial objectives—and the same strategy doesn't necessarily make sense for all of them.

description:
Economics doesn’t have to be complicated.

In this Economics 101 guide, we break down 7 powerful economic principles that affect your money, income, career, businesses, prices, and everyday financial decisions — without complicated graphs, endless equations, or confusing economic jargon.

You’ll learn how incentives shape behavior, why every decision has an opportunity cost, how prices communicate information, what happens when governments introduce price controls, why profits and losses matter, what actually determines your wage, and how comparative advantage makes trade valuable.

The goal isn’t to memorize economic definitions.
It’s to learn how to think like an economist by asking one simple question: What happens next?

In this video, you'll learn:
1. Why people respond to incentives.
2. What opportunity cost really means.
3. How prices act as signals in an economy.
4. Why supply and demand affect the prices you pay.
5. How price ceilings and price floors can create unintended consequences.
6. Why profits and losses provide valuable economic feedback.
7. Why working harder doesn’t automatically mean earning more.
8. How valuable and scarce skills can increase your earning power.
9. Why specialization and trade can benefit both sides.
10. How comparative advantage applies to countries, businesses, and your own life.
11. Why understanding second-order effects can help you make better decisions.

Whether you're learning economics for the first time, trying to improve your financial literacy, or simply want to understand how the economy actually works, this video gives you a practical introduction to some of the most important ideas in economics.

title: How to Manage Your Money LIKE THE 1%
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
How do the wealthy actually manage their money?

It’s easy to look at the top 1% and focus on what they buy — expensive cars, luxury homes, watches and private jets. But those things didn’t make them wealthy — Ownership did.

In this video, we break down a simple 25–15–50–10 money management framework built around one powerful idea:
Use part of what you earn today to build what you’ll own tomorrow.

Instead of spending your paycheck first and trying to invest whatever happens to be left, this approach gives every part of your income a specific job:
25% GROWTH — Building ownership through long-term investing.
15% STABILITY — Building an emergency fund and protecting your finances.
50% ESSENTIALS — Housing, food, insurance, transportation and everyday living.
10% REWARDS — Actually enjoying some of the money you worked for.

These percentages are not official financial rules, and they won’t fit everyone. Your ideal numbers depend on your income, expenses, debt, family situation and financial goals.
The bigger lesson is the order of priority.

You'll learn:
1. Why automatically investing part of your paycheck can be more effective than waiting to see what’s left.
2. Why diversified low-cost index funds can be useful for long-term investors.
3. How an emergency fund can help prevent you from selling investments at the worst possible time.
4. Why controlling major expenses like housing and transportation can matter far more than obsessing over every $3 coffee.

Whether you're trying to start investing, build an emergency fund, contribute more to your 401(k) or Roth IRA, control lifestyle inflation, reach financial independence, or simply get better at managing your paycheck, the goal is the same — Turn more of your income into things you continue to own.

Because looking rich requires money.
Actually building wealth requires ownership.
